Arsenal have been in superb form since the start of the year, turning a season that looked like it would end with a struggle for fourth place into a genuine title push. Coach Arsene Wenger credited Francis Coquelin's consistent defensive work, but downplayed the title talk, saying the win mattered most for keeping the team moving forward.

David Villa, the former Barcelona forward, has made a strong start with New York City FC in the MLS, scoring once and helping his side reach third place in the Eastern Conference. He shared a family photo from the Empire State Building on Instagram, captioning it "Beautiful Empire State Building!!" The newest MLS franchise sits two points behind its city rival, the New York Red Bulls, and Villa will want to secure bragging rights. The club expects a boost from Frank Lampard's arrival at the end of the Premier League season, with New York's next match away to bottom-placed Philadelphia Union on April 11.

Jonjo O'Neill says he is delighted with Shutthefrontdoor, the favourite for the Crabbie's Grand National at Aintree on April 11, which he trains for J P McManus. Although the horse missed a race-day run earlier in the season due to a sinus abscess, O'Neill says he is in peak form and "going to Aintree fresh and well." The big question is whether AP McCoy, who is retiring at the end of the season, will ride him. O'Neill hopes so, calling it a possible fairytale finish, but acknowledges that winning the National is a tall order.

David Villa is settling in well after his move from Europe to Major League Soccer, and he is visiting landmarks around his new home as captain of New York City FC. The expansion club trails its city rival, the New York Red Bulls, by two points, and Villa wants New York City to claim the local bragging rights. The article says the arrival of Frank Lampard, who joins at the end of the Premier League season, will be a major boost and may be the step the club needs to move up.

Trainer Jonjo O'Neill says Shutthefrontdoor, owned by J P McManus, is in top condition for the £1 million Crabbie's Grand National at Aintree on April 11, and it is the race favourite. Jockey AP McCoy, who is about to retire, has not yet confirmed he will ride, but O'Neill expects him to. O'Neill skipped Cheltenham because the horse suits flat tracks better and had a sinus abscess earlier in the season, so the horse is arriving fresh. O'Neill is realistic about the challenge but confident, pointing to the horse's classy, balanced style and his plan to keep it near the front early.

Columnist Dr. Pranav (the author, a brain-injury physician) argues that state lawmakers in Florida and Arizona are improperly dictating medical practice. Florida's 2011 Firearm Owners' Privacy Act bars doctors from asking patients about gun ownership and safety, and Arizona's Bill 1318 requires doctors to tell patients that the abortion pill RU-486 is reversible, a claim the author says is unproven and contrary to mainstream medical guidance. He contends these laws violate patient-doctor communication and that physicians, especially through their specialty groups, the American Medical Association, and state medical societies, should push back more forcefully. He calls on the new U.S. Surgeon General to focus on protecting free communication between doctors and patients.

Harry Kane, 21, called it the "best week of my life" after becoming the youngest Premier League captain this season, a week that also included scoring within seconds of his England debut against Lithuania and making his first England start. His week ended on a frustrating note, as Tottenham were held to a 0-0 draw at Burnley, who earned a valuable point in their fight to avoid relegation. Manager Mauricio Pochettino admitted that a top-four finish is difficult, since Spurs sit seven points behind fourth-placed Manchester City with a much worse goal difference, though he still believes they will try. Burnley boss Sean Dyche felt his side had edged the game and was pleased with another clean sheet against a top team.

Florida's 2011 Firearm Owners' Privacy Act penalizes doctors who ask patients about gun ownership or safety, and it remains in effect while the full 11th Circuit decides whether to hear a challenge to a panel's ruling upholding it. The author says Arizona's Bill 1318 goes further by requiring doctors to make claims about a treatment regimen that most believe to be untrue and unsafe. The author argues these laws turn physicians into government spokespeople and interfere with the patient-doctor relationship. The author also faults state medical associations for not leading the fight, and urges the AMA to use its lobbying resources at the state level and asks Surgeon General Murthy to focus on patient-doctor communication as a public health issue.

Harry Kane, who scored for England and captained Tottenham in his first start for club and country that week, was frustrated as Spurs struggled to break down a hard-working Burnley side, and the match ended in a 0-0 draw. Tottenham manager Mauricio Pochettino admitted that a top-four finish may be out of reach, since they sit seven points behind fourth-placed Manchester City with a much worse goal difference, though he still said his team would try. Pochettino noted that Burnley's long balls into the box made them difficult to play against. Burnley boss Sean Dyche praised Ashley Barnes and was pleased with his side's clean sheet, despite their poor scoring form.

Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott was filmed downing a schooner of beer in seven seconds at a Sydney pub on Saturday, cheered on by a crowd chanting "Skol! Skol!" after a group of Australian rules football players invited him to join them. Some people admired his technique, but others said he was setting a bad example, since Abbott had criticized binge drinking as recently as January 2014. Some social media users also mocked the stunt as a poor imitation of former Prime Minister Bob Hawke's legendary drinking feats.

Former Rangers striker Marco Negri has revealed that he left the club in 2000 because he feared he was HIV-positive. After a leg injury and a reserve-team setback, Scottish tests showed blood anomalies that pointed to a serious condition. In his autobiography, *Moody Blue*, Negri says he returned to Italy for further tests, asked to end his Rangers contract early, and was later told he had only a stress fracture and that his blood was fine. He joined Rangers from Perugia in 1997 for £3.5 million and scored 23 goals in his first 10 league games, but injuries derailed his career at Ibrox.

Former Rangers striker Marco Negri reveals in his autobiography that he left the club after fearing he was HIV-positive. The scare began in 2000, when a crunching tackle in a reserve match against Aberdeen left his right shin bleeding heavily. Months of tests and scans followed, and although the scare was frightening, he was later told in Italy that his blood was completely fine. Negri says the ordeal of waiting for the worst-case diagnosis was a "endless days of terror."

Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott was caught on camera downing a glass of beer in seven seconds at a Sydney pub on Saturday evening, as a crowd of Australian rules football players cheered him on. Observers pointed out the irony, since Abbott had criticized binge drinking as recently as last year, saying he was appalled by the violent binge drinking culture in the country's big cities. Some social media users mocked his effort as a pale imitation of former Prime Minister Bob Hawke, who was credited with drinking two and a half pints in 11 seconds. The story is light-hearted but highlights the contrast between Abbott's public stance on binge drinking and his moment in the pub.

Dove's "One Beautiful Thought" campaign asked a group of women to write down every negative thought they had about their bodies and appearance, then had two actresses read those remarks aloud in a café where the women were sitting within earshot. The women were shocked to hear their private self-criticisms, such as comments about their teeth or arms, spoken by others, and several recognized how harshly they speak to themselves. One woman said she hoped her daughter would never talk to herself that way, and another admitted she says such things to herself all day long. The campaign aims to show that women often bully themselves and to encourage them to be kinder to themselves and to each other, consistent with Dove's earlier efforts such as its #SpeakBeautiful Twitter campaign.

Dove's "One Beautiful Thought" campaign, created in France, asked a group of beautiful women to write down every negative thought they had about themselves. Those thoughts were then turned into a script and read aloud by two undercover actresses seated near the women, who were visibly shocked to hear their private self-criticism repeated back to them. The experiment illustrates how many women bully themselves daily, and the campaign, aired during the pre-Oscars show, urged people to change how they talk about beauty on Twitter, after women sent over five million negative body-image tweets the previous year. It is part of Dove's broader series of videos encouraging women to be kinder to themselves and each other.

Richard Nixon's former San Clemente, California estate, dubbed the "Western White House," is up for sale at $75 million. Nixon bought the 5.45-acre property, built in 1926 and overlooking the Pacific, in 1969 for $1.4 million, and he hosted 17 heads of state there, including Leonid Brezhnev and Henry Kissinger. After his 1974 resignation, he retreated to the home, which he called La Casa Pacifica, and wrote his memoirs there before selling it in 1980 to political ally Gavin S. Herbert. Herbert, now 83, expanded the house over the years and says the decision to sell was "a very hard decision," since he wanted to choose the next "caretakers" carefully.

President Richard Nixon's former San Clemente, California estate, known as the "Western White House," is for sale for $75 million. Nixon bought the 5.45-acre property, built in 1926 and overlooking the Pacific, for $1.4 million in 1969, and he hosted 17 heads of state there. After resigning in 1974 over the Watergate scandal, he retreated to the home, which he called La Casa Pacifica, and he left in 1980. The current owner, Herbert, 83, who has owned the house since buying it from Nixon, says the sale was "a very hard decision" and that he cares about who becomes its next caretakers.

The women's crews will race the same Thames course as the men at the 161st Oxford-Cambridge Boat Race on Saturday, a first that comes 88 years after women were jeered at in the first women's race. The event will be televised for the first time, and Channel 4 presenter Clare Balding gave up her Grand National coverage to host it to highlight the importance of women's sport. Cambridge rower Melissa Wilson is especially moved that her 85-year-old grandfather will be able to watch her compete. The women's race previously took place at Henley over 1.2 miles, and this year's 4.22-mile Putney-to-Mortlake course presents new tactical challenges.

The 161st Oxford-Cambridge Boat Race will give the women's crews equal billing for the first time, racing the same Thames course as the men, who follow an hour later, and the race will be televised for the first time. The change follows decades of campaigning and 88 years after women first raced in 1927 amid jeers and opposition. Cambridge rower Melissa Wilson, 21, recalled being told at 14 that there were no women in the race, and said it was remarkable to be competing on the Tideway, where her grandfather will be able to watch her. Cambridge president Caroline Reid welcomed the move, noting that the early women rowers were pioneers.

Lyon moved back to the top of Ligue 1 for at least 24 hours after a 3-1 win at Guingamp, with goals from Nabil Fekir, a Lacazette penalty, and Clinton N'Jie, while Guingamp's Christophe Kerbrat was sent off before half-time. Montpellier came from behind to beat Bastia 3-1 with two quick second-half penalties, and Lille beat Reims 3-1. Rennes moved closer to survival with a 3-0 win at Lorient, whose own relegation fight took another hit. In the other key results, Modibo Maiga's hat-trick gave Metz a 3-2 win over Toulouse, and Nice and Evian drew 2-2.

Lyon beat Guingamp, with goals from Nabil Fekir and an Alexandre Lacazette penalty, after Guingamp's Christophe Kerbrat was sent off before half-time. The win moved Lyon back above Paris St Germain, who face Marseille on Sunday. Elsewhere, Montpellier came from behind to beat Bastia 3-1 with two quick second-half penalties, and Metz beat relegation rival Toulouse 3-2 thanks to a Modibo Maiga hat-trick. Evian earned a 1-1 draw with Nice late on through an Adrien Thomasson equaliser.

A video crew from the Nepali Pranksters, a comedy group known for hidden-camera pranks, was filming an episode in Nepal when a magnitude-7.8 earthquake struck around 11:55 a.m. on Saturday. Initially assuming it was an ordinary tremor, the team kept filming for 18 minutes as they moved through streets full of crying and shouting people, capturing damage to homes and historic sites such as Dharahara tower and Basantapur Durbar Square, where people were crawling among the ruins. The group and their families survived the first day, but aftershocks and crumbling infrastructure mean that safety remains uncertain.

A magnitude-7.8 earthquake struck Nepal while the Nepali Pranksters were filming an episode of their hidden-camera comedy series in Jawalakhel, near the Central Zoo. The team kept filming for 18 minutes as they moved through streets full of crying and shouting people, documenting destroyed homes, rescues from rubble, and damage to the Dharahara tower and Basantapur Durbar Square. They also urged motorists to clear the roads for emergency vehicles. With aftershocks and crumbling infrastructure still threatening the country, the pranksters and their families survived the first day, but they describe living in fear.

Retired Congressman Barney Frank told a Chicago audience "we're winning" on LGBT rights, even as a California ballot proposal would call for executing gay people and Indiana had just signed a "religious freedom" law allowing businesses to challenge local anti-discrimination protections. The author, a CNN columnist, argues that progress is real compared with a decade ago but that conservative states and 2016 Republican hopefuls, many reluctant to back same-sex marriage, are fueling a renewed "cultural war" over LGBT rights. Ultimately, the author contends, the fight will turn on votes, and the pending Supreme Court ruling on same-sex marriage could shape it. The column concludes that the current climate feels more like defeat than victory.

Former Rep. Barney Frank dismissed a California ballot proposal, which the article calls "The Sodomite Suppression Act" and says would legalize killing gay people, telling an audience "We're winning." Less than a day later, Indiana's governor signed a "religious freedom" law letting businesses challenge local laws that bar discrimination against LGBT customers. The ACLU counts 24 similar bills in 15 states, and the author argues that Republican presidential hopefuls, including Ted Cruz, may push a constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage ahead of an expected Supreme Court ruling. The author concludes that candidates won't be able to avoid taking positions on these measures, despite national polls showing growing acceptance of gay rights.

Percy Sledge, the Alabama-born R&B singer known for his soul classic "When a Man Loves a Woman," has died at age 74 (or unspecified age in the article). His first and biggest hit, recorded in 1966 at Muscle Shoals, became a cornerstone of soul music and was later a UK top 10 hit in 1987. Sledge gave songwriting credit to two members of the Esquires who had helped with a few chords, and he never received royalties from the song, though he considered it the "granddaddy" of all his work. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2005.

Police in Goa, India, arrested four employees of the ethnic-wear chain FabIndia after federal minister Smriti Irani found a security camera pointed at a store's changing room during a visit on Friday. Authorities determined the camera could capture photos of customers, and the four staff members have been charged with voyeurism and breach of privacy, carrying a possible three-year jail term. The store's manager, a woman, was still at large, and police sealed the outlet and summoned six senior FabIndia officials. FabIndia said it was "deeply concerned and shocked" and is investigating internally while cooperating fully with police.

Percy Sledge, the R&B singer known for "When a Man Loves a Woman," died at age 73 in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, of natural causes while in hospice care for cancer. His 1966 debut hit, which he co-wrote and for which he never received songwriting royalties, became a soul standard covered by many artists, including Michael Bolton, who took it to No. 1 in 1991. Sledge also had other hits, such as "Take Time to Know Her" and "It Tears Me Up," and he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2005. His death was followed two weeks later by that of soul singer Ben E. King.

A Marana, Arizona, police officer, Michael Rapiejko, drew scrutiny after he rammed his patrol car into Mario Valencia, an armed suspect who had fired a stolen rifle into the air, and no charges have been filed against him. Court records show Rapiejko had also been sued for excessive force while with the New York Police Department, where a man alleged he was threatened at gunpoint and choked during a 2005 arrest; the case settled for $20,000 with no admission of wrongdoing. Rapiejko resigned from the NYPD in 2006, and the department has not disclosed any disciplinary action. Marana police defend the use of deadly force, while Valencia's attorney says the video shows excessive force against a client who faces 15 charges and survived.

A Marana, Arizona, police officer who intentionally drove his patrol car into an armed suspect, Mario Valencia, previously faced an excessive force lawsuit in New York. A 2005 suit filed by Luis Colon alleged that the officer, Rapiejko, pointed a gun at him, handcuffed him, and choked him during an arrest in front of his family. Rapiejko resigned voluntarily from the NYPD in 2006, and no disciplinary action is known. Valencia survived the crash, was hospitalized, and was criminally charged, while Marana police have defended the officer's actions and the incident has sparked debate over the appropriate use of force.

Police in Goa, India, arrested four employees of the ethnic-wear chain FabIndia after federal education minister Smriti Irani discovered a security camera pointed at the changing room of one of the company's stores during a visit on Friday. Authorities sealed the store and summoned six senior FabIndia officials. The arrested staff face charges of voyeurism and breach of privacy. FabIndia said its officials are traveling to Goa to assist investigators.

Elizabeth Sedway was removed from an Alaska Airlines flight at a Hawaii gate after an airline employee noticed her seated in the handicapped section, asked how she was doing, and then called a medical provider when she said she sometimes felt weak. She said she was pulled off the plane without a doctor's note, despite having cancer, and was left stranded, causing her to miss chemotherapy and her children's school days. Alaska Airlines said its policy is to address medical concerns on the ground, especially on long flights over open ocean, and that its employee acted with the customer's well-being in mind. The airline apologized, admitting the situation could have been handled differently, and refunded her family's tickets and covered their overnight stay.

The author, a former Massachusetts homeland security adviser, reflects on lessons from the 2013 Boston Marathon bombings as the city marks the anniversary. He argues that the terrorism trial of Dzhokhar Tsarnaev showed that the U.S. judicial system can handle terrorism cases, and that the verdict made Tsarnaev a common criminal rather than a mythologized figure. He credits Boston's recovery to competent emergency response, including the swift handling of the crime scene, the absence of deaths among hospitalized victims, and efforts to reunite families. He also identifies problems, such as disorganized command during the Watertown manhunt and inadequate police training for modern weapons, and argues that continued scrutiny is needed to improve future crisis response.

Cardiff City will have no fans at Saturday's Championship match at Elland Road against Leeds United, because the club backed a fan-led boycott and handed back its allocation of 500 tickets. Leeds has not said whether the small allocation came from the club, the council, or the police, and Cardiff CEO Ken Choo said the club was frustrated that its supporters were not given the same freedom of travel that 2,000+ Leeds fans received at Cardiff in November. Cardiff argues that West Yorkshire Police could manage the fixture without restrictions, and the Cardiff City Supporters Club fully endorsed the decision. The club says it would have preferred its fans to attend, but the boycott means Elland Road will have no away supporters for the 3pm kick-off.

Cardiff City will have no fans at Saturday's Championship match at Elland Road against Leeds United, because the club backed a fan-led boycott and returned its allocation of 500 tickets. Leeds has not said whether the small allocation was decided by the club, the council, or the police, and it offered Cardiff far fewer tickets than the 2,000-plus it gave Leeds fans for the reverse fixture, which drew 2,200 Leeds supporters to Cardiff. Cardiff CEO Ken Choo said the travel and ticket restrictions were out of proportion to any risk and that West Yorkshire Police could manage the game without them. Choo also criticized Leeds for refusing Cardiff's request to show the match on a big screen at the Cardiff City Stadium, while the Cardiff Supporters Club said the club's stance sends a message to Leeds about respectful treatment of visiting fans.

A cancer patient, Sedway, was removed from an Alaska Airlines flight at the gate in Hawaii after an employee noticed her in the handicapped section, asked how she was doing, and then consulted a doctor. In a Facebook video, she said she was treated like a criminal or a contagious person for having cancer and no doctor's note to fly. Alaska Airlines said the removal was made with "the customer's well-being" in mind, apologized for the disruption, refunded her family's tickets, and paid for their overnight accommodations. Sedway eventually flew home to California, but said the ordeal would cause her to miss chemotherapy, her children's school, and her husband's meetings.

The author, a former Massachusetts homeland security adviser, reflects on the lessons of the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing and the manhunt that followed. He argues that the trial of Dzhokhar Tsarnaev showed the U.S. justice system can handle terrorism cases, and that the Watertown shootout exposed a dangerous lack of clear police command structure. He also credits the rapid reunification of families with loved ones after the attacks for easing pressure on emergency responders. He concludes that the anniversary should prompt a continued willingness to learn from the tragedy.

One year after the Sewol ferry sank off South Korea's coast on April 16, 2014, killing 304 people, mostly high school students, nine victims remain missing and the wreck is still on the seabed. Families say the disaster's underlying causes, including overloading, improperly secured cargo, an inexperienced crew, and government negligence and corruption, have not been fully addressed. Dozens have been jailed, including the captain, who was sentenced to 36 years, but the promised independent investigation has been stalled by political disputes. President Park Geun-hye has called for salvaging the ship "as soon as possible," though the operation would be technically complex and costly.

Julian Speroni, Crystal Palace's goalkeeper since joining from Dundee in 2004, has triggered a 12-month contract extension that keeps him at the club into a 12th season. He has played a lead role for Palace again this season as they fight to stay in the Premier League. The 35-year-old will also have a testimonial against Dundee at the end of the season. Meanwhile, Palace are looking for a new shirt sponsor after money transfer firm Neteller ended its partnership with the club.

Muhanad Mahmoud Al Farekh, a 29-year-old U.S. citizen with alleged al Qaeda ties, did not enter a plea at his initial court appearance on charges of conspiring to provide material support to terrorists. He was deported from Pakistan to the United States and is accused of plotting to fight American forces abroad and providing support to al Qaeda from 2006 to 2009. Prosecutors say he left Canada for Pakistan in 2007 with two other men, and that one of them, Ferid Imam, allegedly trained three men who planned a suicide attack on the New York subway. If convicted, Farekh faces up to 15 years in prison, and his next court date is May 2.

Julian Speroni has agreed a new contract that will extend his Crystal Palace career into a 12th season, after he triggered a 12-month extension. The goalkeeper, who joined from Dundee in 2004, has once again played a leading role for Palace this season as the club fights to stay in the Premier League. His recent performances include a diving save to deny Yaya Touré against Manchester City on Monday night. He will remain at the club for at least another year.

A Texas-born man, identified as Farekh, appeared in court after being accused of conspiring from 2006 to 2009 to provide material support to al Qaeda and of plotting to fight American forces. He allegedly left Canada for Pakistan in 2007 with two other men, Ferid Imam among them, without telling their families. Prosecutors say Imam later gave weapons and military training at an al Qaeda camp to three men, including Najibullah Zazi. Federal officials described Farekh as a potential threat who could have trained many bombers, and noted that the Justice Department has prosecuted more than 30 similar travel-to-join-terrorists cases in the past 18 months.

The Sewol ferry sank on April 16, 2014, en route to Jeju island, killing 304 people, mostly high school students on a field trip. Investigators cited overloading, an inexperienced crew, and redesigns that added passengers and cargo, and the captain, Lee Joon-seok, was sentenced to 36 years in prison after he was widely condemned for escaping while passengers remained trapped. A year later, the wreck remains on the seabed, and divers stopped searching for the winter. President Park Geun-hye called for its salvage, which families want so investigators can thoroughly examine the accident, but whether it will be raised and an independent investigation held remains unresolved.

Paul Casey, the 99th and final qualifier for the 99-player Masters field, said he was overjoyed to secure the last spot after an anxious wait at his home in Arizona. The 37-year-old, who has made eight Masters appearances, finished sixth on his debut in 2004 and led after five holes of the final round in 2007. Casey said he is excited to return, having missed the experience, and feels better equipped to contend again. He will finish his preparation at the Shell Houston Open, where he won his only PGA Tour title.

Günter Grass, the Nobel Prize-winning author of "The Tin Drum," died at age 87 in a Lübeck clinic, reportedly of pneumonia. His work often explored the horrors of war and genocide through his childhood city of Danzig (now Gdansk), and the Nobel committee praised his mastery of the German language and his surreal, innovative storytelling. His later years were marked by controversy, including his 2006 confession that he had served in the Waffen SS as a teenager and his 2012 poem criticizing German arms sales to Israel. He remained an outspoken critic of politics and current events until the end.

Paul Casey, the 99th and final qualifier for the 99-man Masters field, said he was hugely relieved to secure the last spot, having been projected to fall to 54th at one point during the closing events of the qualifying period. The 37-year-old Englishman, who finished sixth on his debut in 2004 and led after five holes of the 2007 final round, said missing the tournament would have been painful, especially with the season's first major at stake. He added that he is now going into the event wiser after a 2007 penalty incident that affected his round, and he will prepare at the Shell Houston Open, where he won his only PGA Tour title. Tiger Woods' participation remained unconfirmed, although he practiced at Augusta on Tuesday.

Nobel laureate Günter Grass, author of "The Tin Drum," has died, his publisher announced. His work often explored the horrors of war and genocide through memories of his childhood city, Danzig (now Gdansk, Poland). He was also a controversial public figure, known for admitting his youthful service in the Waffen-SS and for a poem criticizing Germany's submarine sales to Israel, which critics called anti-Semitic. Late in life, he remained outspoken, criticizing the anti-Islam PEGIDA movement and proposing that Germans host refugees in their homes.

Chelsea have led or shared the top spot in the Premier League since the opening day and go into their final eight matches seven points clear, starting at QPR. Manager Jose Mourinho praised the club's consistency, stability, and brave approach, but warned that every game remains difficult. He noted that the Premier League is more competitive than Serie A or La Liga and that even top teams routinely drop points, as Manchester City did in their surprise defeat at Crystal Palace. Mourinho will be hoping Chelsea avoid a similar slip at Loftus Road.

Jose Mourinho praised Chelsea's consistency, saying that being top of the Premier League since the first day reflects stability, confidence, and a brave approach. He remained cautious, noting that eight matches remain and that the Premier League can produce dramatic swings in the closing weeks. He argued that the league is more competitive than Serie A or La Liga, and that even top teams lose points. Chelsea will need to avoid slipping up, including at Loftus Road.

An 18-year-old woman, Silhan Ozcelik, has appeared at the Old Bailey, accused of plotting to travel overseas to join Kurdish rebels fighting Islamic State. She went missing from her north London home last October, when she was 17, and allegedly travelled by Eurostar with another man to Stuttgart, Germany, where the Kurdish Workers' Party (PKK) youth movement is based. She is accused of preparing a terrorist attack and was detained at Stansted Airport after returning to the UK in January. She is due to enter pleas on June 12.

An 18-year-old woman, Silhan Ozcelik, from north London has been charged with one count of engaging in preparation for terrorist activity, accused of plotting to join Kurdish rebels fighting the Islamic State. She went missing from her family's home at 17, allegedly travelled to Stuttgart, Germany, where the PKK youth movement is based, and was detained at Stansted Airport when she returned to the UK. At an Old Bailey hearing, she was remanded in custody, with pleas due on June 12 and a trial set for September 7. The PKK, which was founded in 1978 to fight for Kurdish rights in Turkey, is listed as a terrorist organisation by NATO, the US, and the EU.

Raheem Sterling has rejected a new contract at Liverpool, reportedly turning down £100,000 a week, and put off contract talks until the summer. The columnist argues that his explanation for ending the talks doesn't hold up, and that his stance has damaged his standing with fans, especially after Liverpool's hopes of a Champions League place faded in a home defeat to Manchester United. The piece also argues that Sterling, who has played in several positions this season including right wing back, should be more willing to adapt, and that English players are often pigeonholed into fixed roles. It concludes that Sterling should focus less on his contract and more on the kind of versatile footballer who could justify such a salary.

A San Bernardino County man named Pusok was arrested after fleeing deputies on a stolen horse, and a helicopter video showed deputies using a stun gun on him and repeatedly kicking and hitting him after he fell. Sheriff John McMahon called the footage "disturbing" and ordered an internal investigation, and criminal investigations have also begun into the deputies' and the suspect's actions. The sheriff's office said the Taser was ineffective because of Pusok's loose clothing and that a deputy was injured when the horse kicked him. The incident has drawn renewed scrutiny of police use of force, and civil rights groups have said more needs to be done.

Raheem Sterling has turned down a new Liverpool contract and postponed talks until the summer, a decision the columnist argues was poorly judged and has damaged his relationship with supporters. The writer says his stated reasons don't hold up and that his stance is a distraction, since a player's uncertainty about his future doesn't disappear by delaying. Using Liverpool's Brendan Rodgers' tactical switches as a backdrop, the article contends that English players are too rigid about their positions, and that a player earning over £100,000 a week should be willing to play anywhere his team needs him, as Mathieu Flamini and European players have done. The writer concludes that Sterling should focus less on his contract and more on becoming a more versatile player.

The FBI announced it will investigate whether civil rights were violated in a videotaped beating of suspect Francis Pusok by San Bernardino County deputies, who had tried to arrest him after a chase on foot and horseback. The video shows deputies using a stun gun on him and repeatedly kicking and hitting him, and the sheriff opened criminal and internal investigations and placed ten deputies on paid administrative leave. Pusok's attorney and the ACLU of Southern California criticized the force used, with the ACLU saying more was needed on use-of-force and Taser policies. The FBI will forward its findings to federal prosecutors to determine whether charges are warranted.

Santiago Vergini has suggested he may be ready to stay at Sunderland, saying that Premier League survival could bring him a two-year permanent contract. He played a key role in Sunderland's 1-0 derby win over Newcastle, their first victory in nine games in all competitions, which lifted them to 15th place, three points above the relegation zone. Vergini, who joined on loan in January 2014, has said he has felt very comfortable at the club despite its league struggles. The outcome of new head coach Dick Advocaat's effort to keep Sunderland up could significantly shape Vergini's future.

Santiago Vergini says he would be keen to stay at Sunderland, as his contract reportedly includes a clause giving him two more years if the club stays in the Premier League. The 26-year-old Argentinian, on a season-long loan from Costa Rican side Sport Uruguay de Coronado, has made 35 appearances this season, including a start in Sunday's 1-0 derby win over Newcastle. That result, Sunderland's first in nine games in all competitions, lifted the club to 15th place, three points clear of the relegation zone, under new head coach Dick Advocaat. Vergini said he feels comfortable at the club and in the area, though he noted the weather is a downside, and he stressed the need to keep the same spirit in the next match against Crystal Palace.

Record stores are disappearing as large chains like Camelot, Virgin Megastores, and Tower Records have closed, leaving physical music retail mostly to independent shops, often in urban neighborhoods. Many of these remaining stores are thriving by serving passionate customers and collectors, and they function as cultural institutions that celebrate music history, showcase artifacts, and support local music scenes. Record Store Day, held each year, celebrates these shops with live performances, special sales, and other events. The article suggests that music fans should visit these stores, though they may find the staff less than tolerant of casual or mainstream tastes.

Record stores are dwindling in the digital age, but many survivors are thriving by serving a devoted base of customers and collectors. On Record Store Day, hundreds of shops host live performances, signings, rare vinyl sales, and other events. For loyal fans, these stores are cultural institutions that preserve music history, display memorabilia, and support local musicians.

Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe is scheduled to become the first head of the Japanese government to address a joint meeting of the U.S. Congress, an invitation the author considers long overdue given the importance of the U.S.-Japan relationship. The article argues that Abe's visit comes at an opportune time to support the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP), a massive free trade deal among the U.S., Japan, and 10 other Pacific nations that is central to the Obama administration's "pivot" to Asia. The main obstacle is "Fast-Track" trade promotion authority, which must be reauthorized before the TPP can pass, and the House vote is uncertain. The author concludes that Abe faces a difficult task in persuading the American public that the TPP strengthens the alliance rather than outsourcing jobs, especially since many Americans have never heard of him.

Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe's visit to Washington comes at a key moment for the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP), a proposed free trade agreement among the U.S., Japan, and 10 other Pacific nations that together account for about 40% of global GDP. The immediate obstacle in Congress is trade promotion authority ("Fast-Track"), which lets trade deals be voted on without amendment. The Senate will likely pass it, but the House is less certain, partly because some Republicans are reluctant to give the President that power. The article argues that Abe must reframe the debate to convince Americans that the TPP strengthens the U.S.-Japan alliance and counters unfair Chinese trade practices, not just that it creates U.S. jobs, since the outcome will also shape President Obama's "pivot to Asia."

A cheeky monkey in the Thai town of Kanchanaburi was filmed snatching a banana from a female tourist, then slapping her GoPro when she moved in too close. The monkey took a bite, peeled the banana, and ate the rest while its friends watched, and it sniffed the camera lens along the way. When the tourist approached again, the monkey protected its food, raised a hand, and smacked the camera. The footage was captured by the travel couple Maja and Diano, who run a YouTube channel.

A cheeky monkey in the Thai town of Kanchanaburi was caught on camera snatching a banana from a female tourist, then slapping her GoPro when she got too close. The monkey took a bite, peeled the banana, and handed the skin back to her while its friends watched. After she pulled her hand out of the shot and laughed, the monkey sniffed the lens, then protected its food under its arm and swatted the camera. Once the threat had passed, it finished the banana.

MI5 has issued an alert about the threat from "insiders," rogue employees in Britain's nuclear, transport, and public services, following the Germanwings crash, in which co-pilot Andreas Lubitz, who was being treated for depression, deliberately flew the plane into the Alps and killed 150 people. Guidance from the Centre for the Protection of National Infrastructure recommends continuous psychological assessment of key employees, prioritizing those whose jobs pose the greatest risk to the public. A British Airways pilot said the airline does not carry out mental health checks, though BA declined to discuss its health screening. Security sources note that most insider acts come from employees who had no malicious intent when hired but whose loyalties changed later, often after years in the job.

Yorkshire have signed India batsman Cheteshwar Pujara on a deal running until the end of May, after cancelling the contract of Younis Khan, who now hopes to be part of Pakistan's touring party to Bangladesh and so will not play in the County Championship. Pujara, a highly rated Test player with six centuries and nearly 9,000 first-class runs, previously played for Derbyshire and will join Yorkshire once he receives a work permit and Australian Aaron Finch is free of IPL commitments. Yorkshire director of cricket Martyn Moxon said the club moved quickly to sign Pujara, calling him an outstanding young Test cricketer. Pujara said he was eager to return to English county cricket and was proud to wear the white rose once worn by Sachin Tendulkar.

MI5 has warned that rogue employees in Britain's nuclear, transport, and public services pose a serious threat, prompted by the Germanwings crash in which co-pilot Andreas Lubitz, who was being treated for depression, deliberately flew a plane into the Alps and killed 150 people. The warning highlights "insiders," thousands of staff in sensitive roles, and a security source notes that physical safeguards cannot stop someone already inside from committing sabotage or terrorism. The CPNI has identified motives such as theft, revenge, notoriety, ideology, and coercion, and found that these workers often had years of service before turning. Experts argue that employees with higher security clearances should face closer monitoring.

Yorkshire have signed Indian batsman Cheteshwar Pujara until the end of May after cancelling Younis Khan's contract, following Younis's stated intention to pursue international commitments. Yorkshire director of cricket Martyn Moxon said the club moved quickly to secure Pujara, whom he described as a superb player who is looking forward to being part of the club's plans. Pujara, 27, has made six Test centuries since his 2010 debut and is seen by many as the natural successor to Rahul Dravid in India's squad. He will play for Yorkshire until Aaron Finch is available, once he is released from his Indian Premier League commitments with Mumbai Indians.

Brittany Lincicome won her second ANA Inspiration title by beating fellow American Stacy Lewis in a three-hole playoff at Mission Hills Country Club. Lincicome had looked likely to finish among the chasing pack until she made eagle on the par-five 18th to shoot 69 and tie Lewis at nine under par. Lewis then had a chance to win in regulation but missed a 10-foot birdie putt, and the playoff was decided when she bogeyed the third extra hole. The win was Lincicome's first LPGA Tour victory since 2011 and her sixth overall, and she celebrated by jumping into Poppie's Pond, as she had after her 2009 win here.

Brittany Lincicome won her second ANA Inspiration title by beating fellow American Stacy Lewis in a three-hole playoff at Mission Hills Country Club in California. Lincicome was trailing until she made an eagle on the par-five 18th to shoot a closing 69 and tie Lewis at nine under par. Lewis had a chance to win in regulation but missed a short birdie putt, and the playoff ended when her bogey on the third extra hole let Lincicome make par and take the title. The victory was Lincicome's first LPGA Tour win since 2011 and her sixth overall.

DARPA's EXACTO program recently tested "smart bullets," .50-caliber projectiles with optical sensors, in its most successful live-fire round to date, including a case where a novice shooter hit a moving target on the first try. DARPA program manager Jerome Dunn said the system can continuously guide a small-caliber bullet to target, hitting moving and evading targets at sniper ranges that traditional rounds cannot reach. Videos from DARPA show the bullets making sharp midair turns to pursue their targets, and the agency says the technology could also help shooters in high winds. The program aims to improve accuracy at longer distances, allow earlier engagement of targets, and enhance the safety of American troops.

Paul Sturrock suffered a rough start in his first game as Yeovil Town manager, as the club was relegated from League One for the second consecutive time after a 1-1 draw with fellow strugglers Notts County. He had been appointed only two days earlier, though he has previously won promotion five times as a manager. Yeovil had been tipped for promotion this season, but they became the first League One side to be relegated despite ending a six-match losing streak. The result left the club in a difficult position after a disappointing campaign.

Paul Sturrock suffered relegation with Yeovil in his first game in charge, just two days after taking the job, as the club went down for the second consecutive season. The 58-year-old had spent only four days as an advisor to Conference side Torquay before joining League One strugglers Yeovil. Despite a 1-1 draw with fellow strugglers Notts County, where Haydn Hollis's own goal was canceled out by Garry Thompson's equaliser, the Glovers became the first League One side to be relegated. The result was a painful start for Sturrock, who has previously achieved five promotions as a manager.

The U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) reported strong progress on EXACTO, a program developing self-steering .50-caliber "smart bullets" with optical sensors. In February, the bullets passed their most successful live-fire tests to date, hitting moving and evading targets in the hands of an experienced marksman and, notably, a novice shooter. The projectiles can make sharp turns midair, which DARPA says will help shooters hit distant targets, including in high winds. The program aims to improve accuracy at long range, let troops engage targets sooner, and enhance soldier safety.

A three-metre scrub python in Clifton Beach, northern Queensland, was found dead with the remains of a family cat, Tiger, inside its bloated body. Francis Bakvis discovered the snake on Sunday while searching for the 16-year-old cat, which had been missing for three days, and noticed a foul odour in his yard. When he moved the snake, its body broke open, revealing the cat. Bakvis believes the python died after struggling to swallow the cat, which had reportedly slept on the veranda, and he had never seen pythons on the property in 15 years.

A 3.5-metre scrub python in Clifton Beach, northern Queensland, died after trying to swallow the family's 16-year-old cat, Tiger, who had been missing for three days. Owner Francis Bakvis found the bloated snake in his yard on Sunday after noticing a foul smell. When he moved it, the body broke open, revealing the cat's remains. Bakvis believes the python struggled to swallow the cat and died as a result, and he said he had never seen pythons on his property in 15 years of living there.

The New York Yankees and Boston Red Sox are the most-claimed favorite baseball teams in the U.S., ranking first and second, according to a Facebook likes graph that sorted favorite teams by county. The New York Mets, by contrast, get far less support and are not the favorite team in any county. In one county near New York, fans appear to favor the Yankees over the Mets.

Facebook data on profile likes ranks the New York Yankees first and the Boston Red Sox second as the most-claimed favorite baseball teams, with the Texas Rangers and Atlanta Braves also drawing strong regional support in the South. Most teams, however, are favorites only near their home markets, and some, like the New York Mets, win few or no counties at all, since Mets fans in their area often back the Yankees instead. The Toronto Blue Jays dominate most of Canada, while the Yankees and Red Sox also win some areas elsewhere. Outside the Yankees and Red Sox, the San Francisco Giants stand out for their support in Hawaii.

From April 1, anyone can become a football agent by paying a £500 initial one-year registration fee, with £250 renewals each year, though already licensed agents are exempt. The change follows FIFA's decision to leave agent regulation to national associations, and its recommendations include registering only intermediaries of "impeccable character," publishing all deals online, capping agents' fees at three per cent, and barring fees for negotiating deals for players under 18. The Association of Football Agents' chairman, Mel Stein, warns the rules will create "anarchy" and undercut established agents, particularly the fee cap, which he says will destroy the business of about half his members. Clubs and governing bodies share concerns about verifying who is registered, and the FA's registration link was not yet live when the article was written.

From April 1, anyone can become a football agent by paying a £500 initial one-year registration fee, after FIFA stepped back from governing agents. Its recommendations include registering only intermediaries of "impeccable character," publishing all deals annually, capping agents' fees at three per cent, and barring earnings from negotiating deals for players under 18. The FA, Premier League, and Football League have serious concerns about how the system will work in Britain and abroad, especially in under-developed football nations, while the FA says it must follow FIFA's lead. Agents including Mel Stein warn the rules will "create anarchy" and destroy many agents' businesses, and the Association of Football Agents has pushed for self-regulation.

Researchers at the Anne Frank House have found that Anne and her sister Margot Frank likely died at least a month earlier than the previously accepted date of March 1945, which would have been about two weeks after the Bergen-Belsen camp was liberated. Re-examining Red Cross and camp archives along with survivor testimony, they concluded that both sisters were probably sickened by a typhus outbreak that swept through the overcrowded camp, where lice-infested straw and clothing exposed them to the disease. Witnesses reported symptoms before February 7, and since typhus deaths typically occur about twelve days after symptoms appear, the sisters likely did not survive until March. Margot died before Anne, though the exact dates remain unclear.

Gunmen from the Somali militant group Al-Shabaab attacked Garissa University College in Kenya early on a Thursday morning, as prayers were underway, killing nearly 150 people, including students, and wounding dozens more before security forces killed the attackers. The assault followed a deadly attack on non-Muslim quarry workers in Kenya months earlier. Al-Shabaab, which the U.S. designated a foreign terrorist organization in 2008 and which seeks to establish a fundamentalist Islamic state in Somalia, has a history of attacks across the region, including suicide bombings in Uganda in 2010. The article also traces the group's origins, its alliance with al Qaeda, its funding through extortion and taxes, and its recruitment of Americans, particularly from Minnesota's Somali-American community.

New research from the Anne Frank House indicates that Anne and her sister Margot died at least a month earlier than the March 31, 1945 date previously set by Dutch authorities, which means they probably did not survive until the Bergen-Belsen camp was liberated two weeks later. The sisters had been sent to the camp as forced laborers after being separated from their mother, and Anne was exposed to typhus-carrying lice for an extended period. A classmate who saw her there in December 1944 described her as little more than a skeleton. The exact dates of death remain unclear, but Margot died before Anne.

Al-Shabaab, a Somali militant group, has claimed responsibility for a harrowing attack in Nairobi, months after it killed non-Muslim workers at a Kenyan quarry. The group, which the U.S. designated a foreign terrorist organization in 2008, seeks to turn Somalia into a fundamentalist Islamic state and has been behind numerous attacks in the region, including the 2010 Kampala bombings that killed more than 70 people. It has also allied with al Qaeda and recruited Americans, mostly from Minnesota's Somali-American community. The U.S. has supported African Union and U.N.-backed forces fighting the group, though the article notes that Somalia has made some political progress.

Juventus overturned a first-leg 2-1 defeat to beat Fiorentina 3-0 on the night, with goals from Alessandro Matri, Roberto Pereyra, and Leonardo Bonucci, and reached the Coppa Italia final. They did so without Carlos Tevez, Paul Pogba, and Andrea Pirlo, with Tevez ruled out by a thigh injury hours before kick-off. Alvaro Morata was sent off in injury time for a challenge that drew only a yellow card, which means Claudio Marchisio will miss the final through accumulated bookings. Juventus now turn their attention to a Champions League quarter-final against Monaco.

A former iPad owned by Pope Francis sold for $30,500 at Castells, an auction house in Uruguay. The tablet came with a keyboard and a certificate signed by the Pope's personal secretary. It is not the first papal item to fetch a high price, as a motorcycle jacket signed by Francis sold for nearly $68,000.

A iPad once owned by Pope Francis sold at auction in Uruguay for $30,500. It was engraved with "His Holiness Francisco" and "Vatican Internet Service, March 2013" and came with a keyboard and a certificate signed by the Pope's personal secretary. The proceeds will benefit a school in Montevideo, Uruguay. This follows last year's sale of a Harley-Davidson motorcycle the Pope had donated to charity, which fetched $284,000, and a signed Harley jacket that sold for nearly $68,000.

Juventus kept their treble hopes alive by overturning a first-leg 2-1 defeat to Fiorentina, with goals from Alessandro Matri, Roberto Pereyra, and Leonardo Bonucci. Pereyra doubled the lead just before halftime after Fiorentina goalkeeper Neto parried a Alvaro Morata shot into his path. Bonucci, an unlikely scorer, sealed the win shortly before the hour mark with a well-timed volley from a Claudio Marchisio corner. The result sends Juventus to the Coppa Italia final against either Napoli or Lazio, though Marchisio will miss it due to accumulated bookings.

Ian Bell, England batsman and Warwickshire stalwart, has signed a three-year contract extension that keeps him at the club through the 2017 season. He came through the club's youth ranks, debuting for Warwickshire in 1999, and has since played 105 Test matches and 161 one-day internationals for England. Over his career with Warwickshire he has won five trophies, including two County Championships, and has scored 48 centuries in first-class cricket. Warwickshire's director of cricket praised Bell as one of the world's best batsmen and an invaluable squad member, while Bell said he remains eager to achieve more domestically and internationally.

Warwickshire cricketer Ian Bell has signed a new three-year contract with the club, saying he is delighted to remain a "Bear" and still has domestic and international ambitions to fulfil. Bell has won five trophies with Warwickshire, including the County Championship in 2004 and 2012, the B&H Cup in 2002, the Clydesdale Bank 40 in 2010, and the NatWest T20 Blast last season. The club praised him as one of the best batsmen in the world in recent years. Bell is set to leave for England's four-Test tour of the West Indies, ahead of home series against New Zealand and Australia this summer.

Salford Red Devils ended a 17-match losing streak against Wigan with a thrilling 24-18 win, in a game where both sides finished with 12 men. Ben Jones-Bishop scored a spectacular solo try and remains Salford's top scorer, while Michael Dobson was outstanding, scoring a try and setting up two for Niall Evalds. Wigan fought back through a Ryan Hampshire try and Salford sealed the result when Evalds scored his second try four minutes from time. The win was especially sweet for the three former Wigan players in the Salford ranks: Scott Taylor, Harrison Hansen, and Dobson.

Salford Red Devils ended a 17-match losing streak against Wigan with a 24-18 Super League win, with Ben Jones-Bishop scoring a spectacular solo try on the hour to take his seventh of the season. Tries from Larne Patrick, Niall Evalds (two), and Michael Dobson, along with the Red Devils' lead after the break, helped them move into third place, ahead of Wigan. The match was marred by tempers flaring, and both sides finished with 12 men after Weller Hauraki and John Bateman were sent off for trading punches near full time. Salford's victory was their first over Wigan since a 2006 Challenge Cup win, and it was especially sweet for former Wigan players Scott Taylor, Harrison Hansen, and Michael Dobson.

Detroit Tigers pitcher Justin Verlander took a selfie with a young boy wearing a dark blue shirt printed with Verlander's name and jersey number, 35, and posted it to his more than 150,000 Instagram followers. The boy was surprised when he turned around and found the pitcher behind him. The article notes a similar moment in January, when former Philadelphia Phillies pitcher Roy Halladay tweeted a photo of himself with a fan wearing a shirt with his own name and number.

Justin Verlander, pitcher for the Detroit Tigers, took a selfie with a young boy wearing a shirt with Verlander's name and number 35, and posted it to his more than 150,000 Instagram followers. The article also describes a similar moment when former Phillies pitcher Roy Halladay tweeted a photo of himself walking past a fan wearing his jersey, and the fan didn't notice him. In a third example, actor John Stamos visited the San Francisco house from the sitcom *Full House* and took a photo in front of it while fans nearby went unaware of who he was. These stories show how celebrities sometimes surprise unsuspecting fans and share the moments online.

A&E, Lifetime, and History announced a remake of "Roots," the 1977 miniseries about the enslaved African Kunta Kinte and his descendants, which drew over 100 million viewers, to air simultaneously on all three networks in 2016. LeVar Burton, who played Kunta Kinte in the original, is co-executive producer, and the new version will draw more from Alex Haley's novel and consult scholars of African and African-American history. Executive producer Mark Wolper, son of the original's producer, said the story must be retold for each generation, as Kunta Kinte fought to tell his own. Burton added that many young Americans today don't know the story or its importance, which the producers hope the remake will address.

In an announcement, A&E, Lifetime, and History said the three networks will simulcast a new version of "Roots," the epic miniseries about Kunta Kinte, an African captured, enslaved, and sold to a Virginia plantation. The original 1977 series drew over 100 million viewers. The remake will draw more closely on Alex Haley's novel, be described as "original" and "contemporary," and be produced with input from scholars of African and African-American history. The producer, Wolper, framed the project as continuing the story's legacy for a new generation that has seen Barack Obama become president and "12 Years a Slave" win Best Picture, amid ongoing national debate over police treatment of Black suspects.

Louis Jordan, a 37-year-old unemployed truck driver, was rescued after drifting for more than two months in his 35-foot sailboat, which had been capsized and dismasted by a storm just days after he left Conway, South Carolina, to fish. He survived by collecting rainwater, catching fish attracted to his laundry, and rigging a makeshift mast. The crew of the container ship Houston Express spotted his boat hundreds of miles from land and found him signaling for help. Jordan was dehydrated but in surprisingly good condition, and he walked into a Norfolk, Virginia, hospital after being airlifted ashore.

Saudi Arabia resumed airstrikes on Houthi rebel positions in Yemen two days after announcing the end of its month-long air campaign, Operation Decisive Storm. The strikes hit three military compounds in Sanaa and targets in Lahj and Taiz provinces, causing no casualties but destroying the compounds. The resumption followed a Houthi attack on a Yemeni military brigade, and Saudi Arabia said a new initiative, Operation Renewal of Hope, would focus on the political process. The campaign aimed to dislodge the Houthis, who had seized power from the Yemeni government led by President Hadi, and the Houthis released Defense Minister al-Subaihi the day before the strikes resumed.

Saudi Arabia and its coalition partners launched airstrikes against Houthi rebel positions in Yemen on March 26, aiming to oust the Iran-allied group that had overthrown the Yemeni government and seized power. Riyadh announced the end of its nearly month-long campaign, Operation Decisive Storm, but airstrikes resumed less than 24 hours later after Houthi forces attacked a Yemeni military brigade. The Saudis say they want to restore the Yemeni government, and they have outlined next-phase goals that include protecting civilians, expanding humanitarian aid, confronting terrorism, and securing maritime routes. Alongside the military campaign, they are also pursuing a political solution, and a senior Saudi official said the Houthis had agreed to "nearly all demands" of the U.N.

Lifetime will premiere "Grace of Monaco," starring Nicole Kidman as Grace Kelly, on Memorial Day, May 25. The critically panned film, which opened Cannes in 2014, performed poorly internationally, so The Weinstein Co. sold it directly to Lifetime instead of releasing it in U.S. theaters. The movie's troubled path included a dispute between director Olivier Dahan and Harvey Weinstein over the final cut, objections from Grace Kelly's children, and a reduced distribution deal. Tim Roth, Frank Langella, Parker Posey, and Paz Vega also star.

Jordan, an unemployed truck driver, set out from Conway, South Carolina, in his 35-foot sailboat to fish in the ocean, but a storm capsized the boat and broke its mast within days. With a broken shoulder, he rigged a makeshift mast and drifted for more than two months, capsizing twice more and running out of food and water before a container ship crew rescued him. His father had reported him missing on January 29, and Jordan came ashore Thursday evening, dehydrated and hungry but in better condition than many expected. His father said his son, an inexperienced sailor, had been praying throughout the ordeal, which he believes sustained him.

The film *Grace of Monaco*, starring Nicole Kidman as Grace Kelly and directed by Olivier Dahan, was sold directly to Lifetime rather than released in U.S. theaters. It was originally slated for late 2013, but Grace's children criticized it as "needlessly glamorized and historically inaccurate" and boycotted its Cannes premiere. The Weinstein Company later agreed to distribute the film in the U.S. for $3 million upfront, a $2 million discount from its earlier deal, but did not place it in its fall 2015 release schedule.

The article argues that employers, including Koch Industries, Walmart, Target, and Bed Bath & Beyond, should "ban the box" by removing conviction questions from initial job applications so candidates are judged on their skills first. It says these fair-chance hiring policies reduce recidivism, tap an underused labor pool of about 70 million adults with arrest or conviction records, and address racial disparities, since African-Americans are incarcerated at six times the rate of whites and face twice the unemployment rate. The author notes growing bipartisan adoption, with 16 states and over 100 localities having enacted such policies, and urges President Obama to extend the practice to federal contractors. Background checks would still occur, just later in the hiring process.

Koch Industries, Walmart, Target, and Bed Bath & Beyond have adopted "ban the box" policies, which remove conviction-history questions from job applications and postpone background checks until later in hiring. Advocates argue these practices reduce recidivism, reduce stigma, and tap a large pool of talent, since roughly 70 million adults have arrest or conviction records. So far, 16 states and more than 100 cities and counties have adopted fair-chance hiring policies. The author urges President Obama to extend these reforms to federal hiring and to ensure the federal government does not create unnecessary employment barriers for people with records.

Liverpool midfielder Lucas Leiva is returning to fitness after a groin injury that cost him 10 games, and he hopes to regain the form he showed before the injury, when he had made 16 starts in 19 matches. With captain Steven Gerrard suspended for three games and Martin Skrtel also banned, Lucas says the team must cope without them and that he is ready to step in. He turned down time off during the international break to keep his fitness and rhythm, and he feels he is now at 100 percent ahead of Liverpool's Saturday trip to Arsenal.

In this opinion piece, published around the 2015 Persian New Year, the author describes the preliminary nuclear framework between Iran and six world powers as a major step toward a comprehensive deal that would ease sanctions in exchange for guarantees that Iran's nuclear program is peaceful. Many Iranians welcome the agreement as a chance to end their country's isolation and improve an economy they blame on sanctions and the previous government. The author argues that the deal strengthens President Rouhani's moderate administration ahead of the 2016 elections, though his government has not yet improved ordinary Iranians' living conditions. The piece also notes that Supreme Leader Khamenei gave qualified support to the negotiations, which the author calls the biggest chance of rapprochement with Washington since 1979.

The article describes the preliminary agreement between Iran and six world powers (the U.S., Britain, France, Germany, Russia, and China) to continue nuclear negotiations toward a broader deal by the end of June. In exchange for guarantees that Iran's nuclear activities will remain peaceful, the deal would lift sanctions and reintegrate Iran into the international community. The author argues that many Iranians welcome the agreement as a chance to break a long diplomatic impasse, strengthen the moderate Rouhani administration, and possibly improve relations with Washington for the first time since the 1979 revolution. The piece is largely optimistic and frames a full deal as a referendum on the government's foreign policy.

Budae-jjigae, or "army stew," is a Korean dish that emerged during the Korean War, when cooks combined U.S. Army rations like canned, precooked meat (especially SPAM) with kimchi, noodles, and other ingredients. Anthony Bourdain called it a classic example of necessity being the mother of deliciousness. The article includes a recipe for the stew, which uses anchovy-kelp broth, gochujang, gochukaru, and ramen noodles. The dish is also considered a traditional hangover cure.

Lucas Leiva returned from injury and played 90 minutes in Liverpool's All-Star charity game at Anfield, arriving just as captain Steven Gerrard began a three-match suspension for his red card against Manchester United. The Brazilian, who had been a consistent presence before his injury, said Liverpool must show they can cope without key players like Gerrard and Skrtel, and that he is determined to return to his earlier form. He skipped the international break to stay fully fit, having trained for several weeks, and is ready to take on a bigger role during the upcoming Premier League and FA Cup fixtures.

Buddae-jjigae, or "army stew," originated during the scarcity of the Korean War, when cooks improvised with American canned and processed foods. The recipe combines kimchi, hot dogs, baked beans, and ramen noodles with gochujang, gochukaru, and soy sauce in an anchovy-kelp broth. It is simmered for 5 to 10 minutes, with the noodles added near the end, and is typically served with steamed rice or on its own. The article's ingredient list omits the Spam, rice cakes, and ground pork that its instructions mention.

England's Justin Rose has slipped outside the world's top 10 after a poor Florida swing, including three missed cuts and a 55th-place finish at the Cadillac Championship. He spent the past two weeks working on his game, and his first-round 69 at the Shell Houston Open, with 17 of 18 greens hit in regulation, suggested his slump may be temporary. Rose says he corrected faults in his iron play and ball-striking and went back to his old putter. Despite the dip in form, he remains confident about the Masters, where he has often contended and feels comfortable on the course.

Juventus moved closer to a fourth straight Serie A title with a 2-0 win over Empoli, with Carlos Tevez opening the scoring before halftime and Roberto Pereyra adding a stoppage-time second, extending their lead at the top to 14 points with nine games left. Elsewhere, Roma beat Napoli 1-0 to stay second, Lazio won 3-1 at 10-man Cagliari for a seventh straight league win, and Inter drew 1-1 with bottom-placed Parma to a chorus of boos. Cesena came back from 3-0 down to draw 3-3 at Hellas Verona, while AC Milan beat Palermo 2-1 for their first away win since mid-October. The round also included Fiorentina's 2-0 win over Sampdoria, a 2-1 Torino win over Atalanta, and a 1-1 draw between Genoa and Udinese.

Justin Rose, a top-five regular for three years, was struggling with three missed cuts and a 55th-place finish at the Cadillac Championship, and he blamed the Florida swing for exposing his slight misses. He said he had corrected his faults and returned to his old putter, and he stressed that his place in the Masters field was secure despite the dip in rankings. Rose has had a memorable history at Augusta, including leading or sharing the lead after nearly every round, though he threw away a chance to win in 2007 with a double-bogey on the 17th. Meanwhile, Phil Mickelson shot a 66 and Paul Casey a 68 with two eagles, as all three look ahead to the Masters.

Juventus beat Empoli 2-0 on Saturday, with Carlos Tevez scoring just before halftime and Roberto Pereyra adding a second in stoppage time. The win kept them 14 points clear at the top of Serie A with nine games left, putting them on course for a fourth straight league title. The article also covers other results from the same round, including Roma's and Lazio's wins, Roma's 1-0 win over Napoli, and a 3-3 draw between Hellas Verona and Cesena.

Bath travel to Dublin to face Leinster in their Champions Cup quarter-final, hoping to make amends for England's 19-9 Six Nations defeat by Ireland at the Aviva Stadium. Their England players George Ford, Dave Attwood, Jonathan Joseph and Anthony Watson, who all played in that loss, have shared their experience of the venue with the squad. Bath head coach Mike Ford believes that experience, and the confidence from England's strong championship, will help them. The article also profiles key players on both sides, including Leinster's Cian Healy, Jamie Heaslip, Rob Kearney and Sean O'Brien.

Saudi Arabia and its coalition ended "Operation Decisive Storm," a nearly month-long airstrike campaign against the Iranian-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen, and launched a follow-up effort, "Operation Renewal of Hope," focused on a political process. The Saudis say the campaign degraded Houthi military infrastructure and that the Houthis agreed to nearly all U.N. Subject: Would you be willing to be a guest speaker? (No stage fright required!)

Hi [Friend's Name],

I have a favor to ask, and I think you're the perfect person for it. The [Event Name] on [Date] is looking for a guest speaker on [Topic], and I immediately thought of you. Your [specific knowledge/experience/perspective] would be genuinely valuable to the audience.

Here's why I think you should do it:

- **You're more prepared than you think.** You already know this subject deeply. Speaking is just sharing what you know, and you've spent years learning it.
- **Introverts often make great speakers.** You prepare thoroughly, listen carefully, and say things with thought and depth. Audiences often connect with that more than with polished showmanship.
- **The format can be low-pressure.** I can check whether they'd accept a short 10-minute talk, a panel seat instead of a solo presentation, or a conversation with a moderator. You'd also be able to share slides or notes to lean on.
- **It's a finite commitment.** One event, one talk, and then it's over. You don't have to become a public speaker; you just get to share something meaningful once.
- **You'd meet good people.** Attendees and organizers would get to know you, and that kind of connection is hard to find otherwise.

I understand if the idea of standing in front of a crowd feels draining. If it helps, I'm happy to rehearse with you, sit in the front row for moral support, or take on logistics so you can focus on the content. And if after thinking it over you still want to pass, that's completely okay. I'd just hate for you to miss the chance to share something you care about.

Could we grab coffee this week so you can ask questions? Even if you're not sure yet, it would be great to talk it through.

Thanks for considering it,
[Your Name]

The old abandoned house at the end of the street held a secret that no one had ever discovered. Or so the children of Maple Hollow believed, and they had tested the theory for generations.

Every October, the dares began. Someone would climb the rusted gate, pick the lock of the front door with a bobby pin, and run out again before the porch light could flicker on. The house had no porch light, of course. It hadn't worked since before any of them were born. But the legend had its own momentum, and the house kept its silence.

Nell Harrow was eleven when she finally decided to stop listening to the stories and find out for herself.

She went on a gray Tuesday, after school, with a flashlight and a peanut butter sandwich wrapped in wax paper. The front door opened with a groan that seemed to travel down the hall and wake something up. Dust hung in the air, lit gold by the thin light through the boarded windows. There was a staircase, a faded rug, and a smell like old pages and cold rain.

She expected cobwebs and broken furniture. She found those, but she also found a clock on the mantel, its hands stopped at 4:17, and beside it a neat row of spools of thread, each one a different color, arranged by shade from palest cream to deepest blue.

Someone had been here recently. The dust on the spools had been wiped away in a clean circle.

Nell's heart knocked hard against her ribs. She climbed the stairs, one hand on the banister, and found a door at the top of the landing that was slightly ajar. Inside was a small room with a single window and a wooden chair facing it. On the sill sat a jar of buttons, and tacked to the wall above the chair was a map of Maple Hollow, drawn by hand. Every house on the street was marked with a tiny symbol. Some had a check. Some had an X. Hers had a question mark, and it had been drawn in pencil so fresh the graphite still shone.

A floorboard creaked behind her.

Nell spun around, flashlight raised. The hallway was empty. Then she heard it again, soft and deliberate, coming from the room below.

She went down slowly. In the parlor, the clock on the mantel had started ticking. Its hands had moved to 4:18.

On the rug, someone had left a folded note. The handwriting was careful and old-fashioned:

*You were always going to find it, Nell. That is the secret. Every child who comes here finds the house, and the house finds them back. Come again tomorrow. Bring the thread. We still have one color left to finish.*

Nell looked down at the spools, and noticed for the first time that one was missing from the row. A bright, unfinished red.

She heard the clock tick once more, and realized with a shiver that it was keeping time for her.

She didn't run. Not that day. She sat down on the faded rug, unwrapped her sandwich, and waited to see who would come back to the house at the end of the street.
